explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, 'we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.' (2 Corinthians 5:1) He puts a tent on one side and a house on the other. I know which one I'd call home.

A sturdier tent is a nice thought, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says we have 'a building from God, an eternal house in heaven' (2 Corinthians 5:1). That's not a tent with better stakes. It's like offering someone a nicer paper cup when there's a whole bakery waiting for them.

explanations.answer: A longer stay in this tent
explanations.explanation: Paul isn't offering an extension on the tent, friend. He says, 'if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven' (2 Corinthians 5:1). So what comes after the tent is a house, not more tent. No late checkout here.

Paul says the opposite, friend. The house is 'not built by human hands.' (2 Corinthians 5:1) It's 'a building from God.' Every cooling rack in my bakery was built by human hands, and every one of them wobbles.

Right, and Paul says it plainly: 'not built by human hands.' (2 Corinthians 5:1) It's a building from God, an eternal house in heaven. With no human crew, nobody gets to argue about the paint color. I like those odds.

explanations.answer: To be clothed with our heavenly dwelling
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Paul says, 'in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling.' (2 Corinthians 5:2) The groan and the longing sit side by side in one verse. And the longing has an address: our heavenly dwelling.

explanations.answer: To keep living in this earthly tent
explanations.explanation: Paul's longing points the other direction, baker. He says, 'in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling.' (2 Corinthians 5:2) The tent is where the groaning happens, and the longing is for the heavenly dwelling. Nobody's mailing a postcard asking for more tent.

explanations.answer: To forget the troubles of this life
explanations.explanation: Paul does talk about burdens (2 Corinthians 5:4), but he never talks about forgetting them. His longing here is 'to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling' (2 Corinthians 5:2). Forgetting is how I handle where I put my spatula, and it has never once been a plan.

Yes. Paul says, 'when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.' (2 Corinthians 5:3) He keeps the clothing picture going from verse 2, where we're longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling. It's a short verse, and it hangs on that one word.

It's an easy one to reach for, I think, since all that groaning could sound lonely. But Paul's word in this verse is different: 'when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.' (2 Corinthians 5:3) He stays with the clothing picture from verse 2. Alone isn't a word he uses here.

Lost fits the mood, I think, but it isn't Paul's word. He says, 'when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.' (2 Corinthians 5:3) The clothing picture from verse 2 carries right on into this verse. Same picture, one new word.

That's right. Paul says, 'we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed.' (2 Corinthians 5:4) Count the pieces: the groaning, the burdens, and the wish to be clothed. All three are in that one verse, and you caught every one.

This one is stated outright, friend. Paul says, 'we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed.' (2 Corinthians 5:4) So the wish is to be clothed, and he says it straight. It's easy to second-guess when a sentence has this many moving parts. I've second-guessed recipes with fewer.

You nailed it, baker. Paul says, 'so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life.' (2 Corinthians 5:4) Mortality is the thing getting swallowed, and life does the swallowing. I love a sentence where the good thing gets the last word.

Time feels right to me too, since it swallows my whole afternoon every time I start a batch. But Paul says, 'so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life.' (2 Corinthians 5:4) Mortality is what gets swallowed, and life is what does it. Time doesn't get a spot in this sentence.

Sorrow would turn that into a gloomy sentence, friend, but Paul closes it differently. He says, 'so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life.' (2 Corinthians 5:4) The word he lands on is life. Life is the only thing in this verse doing the swallowing.

Yes, the Spirit. Paul says, 'it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.' (2 Corinthians 5:5) God is the one who gives it. And the pledge points ahead to what is to come.

Angels are impressive, I'll give you that. But Paul says God 'has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.' (2 Corinthians 5:5) The Spirit is the gift in this verse. No angel gets a mention here.

Rainbow is my favorite color, so I wanted that one to win too, friend. But Paul says God 'has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.' (2 Corinthians 5:5) The Spirit is the pledge in this verse. The rainbow will have to wait for another passage.

That's right. Paul says, 'we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 5:6) Always, baker. Not most days, and not only when the dough rises.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, 'we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 5:6) The confidence and the away part sit in the very same sentence. And that word 'always' is right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: By faith and not by sight
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, 'we walk by faith, not by sight.' (2 Corinthians 5:7) I spent years in a dark junk drawer, and sight was not an option. Mostly I bumped into rubber bands.

explanations.answer: By sight and not by faith
explanations.explanation: That's the recipe with the ingredients swapped, friend. Paul says, 'we walk by faith, not by sight.' (2 Corinthians 5:7) Faith comes first, and sight is the one he sets aside. Same two words, flipped, and it changes the whole batch.

Paul doesn't mention strength in this verse. He says, 'we walk by faith, not by sight.' (2 Corinthians 5:7) The two things he sets side by side are faith and sight. Strength never shows up, and mine gives out halfway through stirring dough anyway.

Yes. Paul says, 'We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 5:8) The confidence from verse 6 carries right into this verse. Prefer is a gentle word, and it's the one he chose.

Refuse is a strong word, and Paul doesn't reach for it. He says we 'would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 5:8) I can't even refuse the last cookie, and I'm the one in charge of the cookies. His word is prefer.

Dread is a heavy word, friend, and Paul doesn't use it here. He says we 'would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 5:8) Dread is how I feel about scrubbing the mixing bowls. Paul's verse starts with 'We are confident,' and that's the mood it keeps.

You got it, baker. Paul says, 'we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it.' (2 Corinthians 5:9) Here or there, the aim stays the same. I like an aim that travels well.

Rest sounds great after a long day at the oven, and I won't argue. But Paul says, 'we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it.' (2 Corinthians 5:9) The aim in this verse is pleasing Him. Rest doesn't make the list.

Praise from others feels nice, I'll admit it, because I light up when someone compliments a batch. But Paul says, 'we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it.' (2 Corinthians 5:9) The one he wants to please is Him, not the crowd. Different audience entirely.

explanations.answer: Before the judgment seat of Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says, 'we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.' (2 Corinthians 5:10) Notice the word 'all.' And he writes 'we,' so he counts himself in with everybody else.

That sounds like a place with real seats, baker, but Paul doesn't name it here. He says, 'we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.' (2 Corinthians 5:10) The seat belongs to Christ. And he says 'all,' so no one is left out of that sentence.

Caesar's name doesn't show up in this verse, friend. Paul says, 'we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.' (2 Corinthians 5:10) The seat is Christ's. The 'all' in that sentence covers every one of us.

Paul says more than that, friend. He says each one may receive his due 'for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.' (2 Corinthians 5:10) The word 'only' isn't in the verse. Both kinds of things are named, and he says 'each one,' so it's about every person.

That's right, baker. Paul says, 'each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.' (2 Corinthians 5:10) So the verse covers both, not just the good. He says 'each one,' so it's about every person. It's a serious verse, and I read it slowly.
